howto.name: Meet the basic requirements
howto.text: Be at least 18 years old with a high school diploma or equivalent and a U.S. Social Security number.

howto.name: Complete the 63-hour pre-license course
howto.text: Finish Florida's state-approved 63-hour sales associate pre-license course and pass its end-of-course exam.

howto.name: Get fingerprinted
howto.text: Submit electronic fingerprints through a state-approved vendor so Florida can run your background check.

howto.name: Apply to the DBPR
howto.text: Submit your license application to the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation and receive exam authorization.

howto.name: Pass the Florida state exam
howto.text: Pass the 100-question Florida sales associate exam with a score of 75% or higher at a Pearson VUE testing center.

howto.name: Activate your license under a broker
howto.text: Join a licensed Florida broker, such as Adams, Cameron & Co. in Daytona Beach, to activate your license and start working with clients.

If you’re thinking about getting your real estate license in Daytona Beach, two questions actually matter: how do you get licensed, and is this a market worth building a career in? Here are honest answers to both, with real local numbers, not brochure language.

How do you get a real estate license in Daytona Beach?

There’s no separate “Daytona Beach license.” You earn a Florida real estate sales associate license, valid statewide, then work locally. The path is the same everywhere in Florida:

  • Be at least 18 with a high school diploma or equivalent;
  • Complete the state-required 63-hour pre-license course;
  • Get fingerprinted for your background check;
  • Apply to the DBPR and pass the state exam (75% to pass); and
  • Activate your license under a broker: you can’t practice on your own.

Each step is covered in detail in our step-by-step Florida licensing guide. Most people finish in two to four months.

Is Daytona Beach a good market for a new real estate agent?

Daytona Beach is a steady, balanced market, not a frenzy, and for a new agent that’s good news. The median home sells for around $320,000, takes roughly 77 days to sell, and receives about two offers. Translation: homes don’t vanish in a weekend bidding war, so the agents who win are the ones who actually know the market and stay in front of clients, not whoever happens to be fastest. That’s a market a well-trained newcomer can break into.

Across Volusia County, roughly 900 homes change hands every month at about a $343,000 median, and inventory has climbed sharply, with active listings up an estimated 50–70% in areas like Daytona Beach and Deltona. More listings means more property to show, more sellers who need representation, and more room for a new agent to find a lane: beachside condos on the barrier island, mainland single-family homes across the Halifax River, and steady relocation and second-home demand from out of state.

Where is the real estate growth near Daytona Beach?

Just up the coast, Flagler County is the sixth-fastest-growing county in Florida. It added about 25,000 residents between 2020 and 2025 (a 21.7% jump) to reach roughly 140,000 people. Palm Coast’s median is around $349,000, and the city recently approved 533 new single-family homes in one batch of developments. For an agent based in the Daytona area, that growth is a 30-minute drive away, which is exactly why a brokerage with offices across both counties matters.

Does the brokerage you start with really matter?

Your Florida license has to be held by a broker, so your first real decision isn’t a neighborhood, it’s a brokerage. And the competition is real: Adams, Cameron & Co. alone has around 300 agents, and that’s one firm in a county full of them. A new agent without training, tools, and mentorship gets out-marketed quickly. A new agent with all three gets traction. That gap, not talent, is why similar people thrive at one brokerage and wash out of the business at another within 18 months.

Why start your real estate career with Adams, Cameron & Co.?

Adams, Cameron & Co. has been the Daytona Beach area’s largest brokerage since 1963, the most recognized real estate name in Volusia and Flagler County. For a new agent, that history is leverage: when you introduce yourself with the Adams Cameron name, sellers already know it and trust it.

It’s also genuinely local across the whole market, with offices in Daytona Beach (600 S. Atlantic Ave), Ormond Beach, Port Orange, DeLand, and Palm Coast, so wherever the next deal is, there’s a desk and a manager nearby. New agents get the support that determines whether year one works:

  • In-house marketing and technology at no cost, so your first listing looks professional;
  • Non-competing managers with access seven days a week (they don’t list against you);
  • Mentorship and training built for people brand new to the business; and
  • A global referral network: as a member of Leading Real Estate Companies of the World, the brokerage connects local agents to referrals across 70+ countries.

What is the next step to become an agent in Daytona Beach?

If you’re seriously considering it, do two things: read the licensing guide so you know exactly what’s ahead, and start a conversation with Adams, Cameron & Co. about launching in Daytona Beach. Go deeper on the town’s real story in our full history of Daytona Beach. Weighing Ormond Beach too? See our honest Daytona Beach vs. Ormond Beach comparison first. No pressure, just a clear picture of the path and the support you’d have on it.

faq.q: Do I need a special license to sell real estate in Daytona Beach?
faq.a: No. You need a Florida real estate sales associate license, which is valid statewide. You complete Florida's process: a 63-hour course, the state exam, and a background check. Then work locally in Daytona Beach under a broker.

faq.q: Is Daytona Beach a good market for a new real estate agent?
faq.a: Yes, and partly because it's balanced rather than frantic. The median home is around $320,000 and takes about 77 days to sell, so success comes from knowing the market and staying in front of clients, something a well-trained new agent can do. Volusia County sells roughly 900 homes a month, and fast-growing Flagler County is right next door.

faq.q: How much do real estate agents make in the Daytona Beach area?
faq.a: Real estate income is commission-based, so it varies widely with how much you sell. With a Volusia County median around $343,000 and roughly 900 sales a month, there's real volume to work, but a new agent's first-year income depends heavily on training, lead support, and the brokerage behind them.

faq.q: How long does it take to become an agent in Daytona Beach?
faq.a: Typically two to four months: the time to complete Florida's 63-hour course, pass the state exam, and activate your license under a broker. After that you can begin working with clients right away.

faq.q: Which brokerage should a new agent join in Daytona Beach?
faq.a: Look for training, mentorship, marketing tools, and broker access. Adams, Cameron & Co. has been the Daytona Beach area's largest brokerage since 1963, has around 300 agents and offices across Volusia and Flagler County, and gives new agents in-house marketing, seven-day non-competing manager support, and tools at no cost.
